title: An icon drawn in a frame exports as a still picture instead of an animated SVG
goal: Draw an icon inside an icon frame, give something in it a motion, and export it as an Animated SVG: the file that comes out is one still photograph of the icon with no animation in it at all. The tutorials tell you to start on an icon frame and then to export an animated SVG, so following both in order hands you a file that does not move. The Export sheet warns that the frame rides along as a picture but never says the motion was thrown away.
acceptance: An icon drawn inside an icon frame, with one piece of it moving, exports as an Animated SVG that moves when opened in a browser
That file carries no embedded picture when everything in the frame is shapes
Anything the file still cannot carry is named in the Export sheet before you save
A test exports a frame holding a moving piece and asserts the written file has animation elements in it

log.note: Before building: weighed the two answers in the notes. Exporting the frame's CHILDREN as the document would lose the cut (a piece hanging off the edge would appear in the file, which is not what the canvas shows) and would lose the frame's own rounding. Writing the cut as a <clipPath> keeps both and fixes the whole-canvas export too, not just the frame-scoped one. Built that.

Shipped: SVGExport.answer no longer sends a clipping group to the picture path; Writer.cutBox/defineCut write a <clipPath> of the group's box (rounded where the corners are) and hold surface + children in one <g clip-path>, with the border ring outside it so a ring is painted over the edge rather than cut by it. A group with rounded corners cuts too, since DocumentRenderer.groupImage already does. Layers moving INSIDE something that still goes out as a picture are now named in result.unmoved, so the Export sheet says which piece stopped moving. PhotonzDocument.frameDocument carries motionCycleMS, so one frame exported on its own loops at the length the canvas plays it at.

Verified in a real browser, which is what acceptance 1 asks for. Wrote a throwaway test that exports a 32pt icon frame (rounded 6, white surface, a red bar hanging off the edge, a blue dot sliding 4 to 20 over 700ms in a 1400ms lap) to /tmp/photonz-icon.svg, then opened it in Chrome. The file: no base64, no fallbacks, no unmoved, one <clipPath id=clip-1><rect 0 0 32 32 rx=6> and one <animateTransform>. In Chrome, with the SVG inlined and scaled 10x by CSS: the dot's centre reads 8, 16, 24, 16, 8 icon units at t=0/0.175/0.35/0.525/0.7 and loops, all four corners are cut round (elementFromPoint 8px in from each corner hits the page, 70px in hits the white surface), and the red bar paints only as far as the frame's edge. Screenshot saved as queue/audits/2026-09-16-icon-export-1.png. First attempt at this check was wrong and worth recording: scaling the markup with sed also rewrote the clipPath rect's own width and height, which made three corners look square. Scale with CSS, never by editing the file.

Could not run any walk: the Mac's screen was locked for the whole task (probe-app.sh said so on its Grants line), so a walk finds no control by name and refuses. Asked for a sweep instead. left rough: a frame at the canvas origin writes an empty <g> round itself, since a group at the origin gets no transform and the clip now sits on a group of its own inside it. Noise in a file meant to be readable, invisible to anyone who is not reading the markup, and true of every group at the origin rather than anything this change introduced, so no task.

A clipping group (which every icon frame is) now writes a <clipPath> instead of falling back to one embedded PNG, so an icon drawn in a frame exports as shapes that move. Motions baked inside anything that still goes out as a picture are named in the Export sheet's warning line, and one frame exported on its own keeps the document's lap. Verified: 7781 tests pass (Scripts/test.sh), including new render-back comparisons that draw the exported file through the system's SVG reader and check it matches the canvas, and a real browser check in Chrome where the dot animates, the corners cut round and the overhang is clipped (queue/audits/2026-09-16-icon-export-1.png).
